item.title: Finding Freedom from Fear: A Christian Counselor’s Personal Story
item.description:
Fear is an essential survival mechanism that elicits both physical and emotional reactions. When you sense a threat, fear is protective. However, fear can be overwhelming if it is out of balance and out of proportion to the risks. Maintaining psychological balance requires an understanding of the nature of fear and practical coping strategies.

For God has not given us a spirit of fear, but of power and of love and of a sound mind – 2 Tim. 1:7, NKJV

My Journey Into Fear

Personally, I spent years living in fear. As a child, I was afraid of the dark. Fear followed me into adulthood, marriage, moving to a bigger city, then motherhood, and my home. Although I loved God and trusted Him, I couldn’t seem to silence the constant “what ifs” that stole my peace.

One thing that magnified my fears was the news. As long as I can remember, I’ve noticed a trend on the news and then eventually on social media: fear.

There is always something on the news or happening in the world that could make us fearful: wars, pandemics, health issues, job insecurity, the health and welfare of our children, other anxieties and phobias, etc. I got sucked into the news after 9/11. So, in 2020, after the news of the pandemic, I had to stop watching or reading the news.

I had faith; I believed in God, and deep down I knew He would protect us. But I couldn’t shake that grip that fear had on me. I would pray over our house, walk around and pray over our property, etc., but nothing seemed to help the fear subside.

I had trouble sleeping because of my fears of someone breaking into our home. I bought a little picture of an angel guarding a child’s bed and every night began to recite the passage that was printed on it: Psalm 4:8, “In peace I will lie down and sleep, for you alone, LORD, make me dwell in safety.”

I had been reading The Power of a Praying Parent by Stormie Omartian and read the chapter on fear, not just for my daughter, but for me. It was pretty humbling. I tried to read other books on fear, but they all dealt with things such as stage fright, asking for a raise, etc. Those are still real and debilitating fears, but I felt like I was the only person who was fearing for my life.

A Prisoner of Fear

Looking back, I realize I was truly a prisoner to my own mind and emotions. On top of the fear, I was dealing with so many other “issues.” God began to slowly peel away at those issues one by one, but it truly took faith to overcome the fear.

Neil T. Anderson (2017) reminds us, “Fear is a God-given natural response when our physical or psychological safety is threatened. Fear always has an object, that is something or someone, and that object must be both present and potent, that is perceived to have some power over us. It ceases to be a fear object when only one of those attributes is eliminated” (p. 28).

He goes on to explain, The fear of people, death, and Satan is the root of almost all fears. Death is still present since it is a real possibility, but once we believe in Jesus and accept Him as our Lord and Savior, it is no longer powerful (1 Cor. 15:54-55).

Although fear is a normal human reaction, sometimes anxiety and fear become more than occasional worry. I realize that, for some individuals, anxiety can involve biological, psychological, and environmental factors that require additional support. But for now, I am talking mostly about fear that is out of balance and has no real threat.

In counseling, we often talk about how our thoughts influence our emotions and behaviors. Fear thrives on repeated messages of danger, while faith grows when we intentionally focus on truth. Another perspective that helped me was understanding fear as misplaced faith – placing belief in what might go wrong rather than in God’s promises.

Looking back, I can see how fear grew stronger when I repeatedly focused on threatening information. The more I watched the news and imagined worst-case scenarios, the more my mind became trained to anticipate danger.

The Nature of Fear

As a counselor, I have seen how anxiety can affect even the strongest believers. Experiencing anxiety does not mean someone lacks faith, nor does seeking counseling, medical care, or medication indicate spiritual weakness.

God often works through the wisdom, support, and resources He provides through others. Just as we seek treatment for physical illnesses, there are times when receiving professional support for our mental and emotional well-being is an important part of healing.

One resource God used during my journey was a small booklet called Freedom From Fear. While I don’t believe one book is the answer for everyone, God used its biblical perspective to help me recognize how fear had shaped my thinking. For some reason, reading it made that little lightbulb in my brain turn on. I had that “Aha” moment.

“There are two spiritual laws at work in the world today: the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus and the law of sin and death. The force of faith comes from life. The force of fear comes from death” (back cover). In the booklet, the law of reciprocals (“corresponding, but reversed or inverted” principles) is discussed in Romans 8:2: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death.”

Understanding that fear is just faith perverted (by Satan) opened my eyes. Satan is “limited to the forces of the world.” He cannot create or come up with new ideas. He just perverts the spiritual laws that are already in place. “Sin was not a new law. It was righteousness perverted. Death was life perverted. Hate was love perverted. Fear was faith perverted (pg. 5).”

In the Garden of Eden, after Adam and Eve sinned, the first words Adam spoke to God were, “I was afraid” (Genesis 3:10). The enemy is here to steal, kill, and destroy. So, he took the faith that Adam had, and it was turned to fear. I love where it’s explained, “The counterfeit never is as powerful as the real thing” (pg. 7). Therefore, we know that when we put faith to work, “it will always overcome fear.”

The Complexity of Anxiety and Fear

As I reflect on those years, I also recognize that fear and anxiety can be complex. While my journey involved learning to trust God more deeply and renew my mind with His Word, I realize that not everyone experiences fear in the same way.

Some people have lived through traumatic events, loss, abuse, or other painful experiences that leave their nervous system on high alert. Others struggle with anxiety disorders, panic attacks, obsessive thoughts, or other mental health concerns that involve biological, emotional, and environmental factors.

Practical Steps When Fear Feels Overwhelming

  • Identify the fearful thought.
  • Ask whether there is evidence of an actual present danger.
  • Compare that thought with God’s truth in Scripture.
  • Pray honestly about your fears.
  • Pray specific and related scriptures out loud (I will list some below).
  • Reach out to trusted believers or a counselor when fear becomes persistent or overwhelming.
  • Limit media that continually fuels fear.
  • Remember that courage often means moving forward while still feeling afraid.

For me, freedom came through prayer, Scripture, renewing my mind through books and other resources, and learning to trust God’s promises. For others, that journey may also include counseling, support groups, trauma work, medical care, or a combination of these resources. God can use all of these tools as part of His healing process.

But in our everyday Christian walk, we have to walk by faith. In doing so, we have to know the Word of God and stand on its principles. We have to know that Satan is under our feet because of what Jesus has done for us. As believers, we are free from every part of the curse.

So, why do we allow him to pull us around on strings of fear, worry, anxiety, depression, etc.? Yes, we are physical beings and will have physical problems, but God is bigger than any of our problems, and He has put other people – professionals – here on earth to help us walk through some of the pains of life.

Even though we know these truths, many of us still wrestle with fear, worry, anxiety, and discouragement. Sometimes these struggles are connected to painful experiences, ingrained thought patterns, or circumstances beyond our control. Yet God’s promises remain true. He meets us in our struggles and patiently helps us grow in faith as we learn to trust Him more fully.

For believers, Scripture is the foundation for confronting fear – both the fears rooted in reality and the ones shaped by our thoughts and emotions. God can also place different resources in our paths to help us confront fear and work through the layered process of renewing the mind. We can’t just stop at reading the Scripture; we have to believe it and apply it.

James 1:22 tells us, “But don’t just listen to God’s word. You must do what it says.” We have to speak the Word and believe what we are saying. When we speak His promises, we must remember the authority that we have through Jesus and speak it with confidence, not with hesitation.

As believers, we must take every thought captive (2 Cor. 10:5). Then, we must renew our minds with the Word of God (Rom. 12:2). I will share some of my favorite passages below. 365 references in the Bible say or address, “Do not fear.” Or as one of our friends says, “One ‘Do not fear’ for every day of the year!” (I love that!)

After I read Freedom from Fear, I knew that things were beginning to change in my thought life, but it wasn’t until a women’s retreat (my first retreat with my church) that I truly became free and broke off the chains of fear. I had gone to get away, enjoy myself, and, of course, for the great teaching I would receive, but I didn’t realize it would be life-changing.

I went away still battling fear, but returned home freed from the hurts, bitterness, worry, and the rest of the lies the enemy had been telling me at that time.

Fear once dictated many of my decisions, stole my peace, and kept me awake at night. Today, I still face circumstances that could make me fearful, but I no longer live under fear’s control. Freedom did not come overnight; it came through renewing my mind with God’s Word, learning to trust Him more deeply, and choosing faith one step at a time.

Anderson (2017) says, “Courage is not the absence of fear. Courage is choosing to live by faith and doing what is right in the face of perceived fear-objects. Behind every irrational fear is a lie, which must be identified. Ask the Lord to reveal to your mind the nature of your fears and the irrational lies that compel them” (2017, p. 28).

If fear has become a constant companion in your life, know that you are not alone. Whether through prayer, Scripture, counseling, supportive relationships, or a combination of these resources, healing is possible. The Lord is for you. And because He is for you, fear does not have to have the final word.

As I’ve shared, freedom from fear did not happen overnight for me. It was a process of learning to recognize fearful thoughts, replacing them with truth, and choosing – sometimes moment by moment – to trust God. Healing often works the same way. It may involve different resources that God provides. While the journey looks different for each person, we can take comfort in knowing that God walks with us through every step.

Bible Verses to Ponder

The LORD is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The LORD is the strength of my life; of whom shall I be afraid? When evildoers came upon me to devour my flesh, my adversaries and my enemies, they stumbled and fell. Though a host encamp against me, my heart will not fear; Though war arises against me, in spite of this I shall be confident. – Psalm 27:1-3, NKJV

The LORD is for me; I will not fear; What can man do to me? – Psalm 118:6, NASB

Don’t be afraid of those who want to kill your body; they cannot touch your soul. Fear (reverence) only God, who can destroy both soul and body in hell. But the very hairs of your head are all numbered. so do not fear; you are more valuable than many sparrows. – Matthew 10:28, 30-31, NLT

Since the children have flesh and blood, he too shared in their humanity so that by his death he might break the power of him who holds the power of death – that is, the devil –  and free those who all their lives were held in slavery by their fear of death. – Hebrews 2:14-15, NIV

Seeking support is not a sign of weak faith. God often works through the wisdom, support, and resources He provides through others. Please give our reception team a call and schedule an appointment.

References: 
Anderson, N. T. (2017). The steps to freedom in Christ: A biblical guide to help you resolve personal and spiritual conflicts and become a fruitful disciple of Jesus. Bethany House Publishers
Kenneth Copeland. (1997). Freedom from fear. Kenneth Copeland Publications.

item.title: Overwhelming Anxiety in a Time of War: Finding Solid Ground Through Faith
item.description:
Here we are again. Breaking news, a new conflict has erupted in a distant land. We are glued to our televisions, computers, or smartphones, drawn in by a relentless news cycle that bring the unnerving feeling of uncertainty in a world that seems to be in constant turmoil.

As a chaplain in the Army Reserves and throughout my 21-year Army career, the all too familiar phone calls from friends and loved ones panicking over a news story of new conflict have been a frequent reminder that overwhelming anxiety during times of war impact those I love the most more than me.

We live in an age when technology keeps us connected to conflicts, even though they happen far away. We find the weight of what’s unfolding in the world, settling into our homes as if it is there to take charge. This can bring about anxiety, especially during war.

Wartime stress isn’t confined to the battlefield or the families waiting by the phone. It will creep into ordinary life, the grocery store, the drive to work, and even in the moments before sleep. Overwhelming anxiety in the middle of a global conflict is real, valid, and something that far more people of faith grapple with than most of us are willing to admit.

Wartime stress can feel invisible from the inside, even as everything on the outside looks completely normal. We go to work. We show up for our family and sit in the pews on Sunday morning. In fact, as pastor of a local church, there have been times when I have to walk in on a Sunday morning with more questions than answers about conflicts erupting around the world.

At times I wonder, Will it be me called up to go next while at the same time trying to reassure my family, friends, and congregants? The reality is that underneath all the functioning is something that feels increasingly fragile. If you feel like this, you’re not alone, and you’re not without hope.

The Lord is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. – Psalm 23:1–3, ESV

What Wartime Stress Actually Does to You

Our nervous system was not designed to absorb a continuous stream of crises. Still, with today’s technology, that is what happens: conflict dominates the news cycle and social media feeds. It leads to the sense that the world is unstable. Even though we’re not in a war zone, our bodies respond to this threat in measurable ways.

Our sleep becomes unreliable, and our concentration slips. We find that we’re easily startled and emotionally short-tempered with the people we love at the end of the day. We are exhausted beyond the point where rest can fix it. We find ourselves constantly hooked on scrolling through the feeds for updates and news.

We think that being constantly informed is a way of restoring a sense of control, even when we have no direct connection to the conflict. Compassion fatigue and secondary trauma are real. The grief we experience when we watch human suffering from a distance lands somewhere in the body and the mind, and does not dissolve simply because you step away from the computer or set down the phone.

For Christians, there’s an additional weight that comes in the quiet voice whispering that feeling afraid means you’re not trusting God. This internal pressure adds to the weight of the stress that we already carry simply because we care. Even in this, we can rest in God’s protection:

For he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble; he will conceal me under the cover of his tent; he will lift me high upon a rock. – Psalm 27:5, ESV

When Overwhelming Anxiety Becomes a Daily Reality

There is a difference between feeling concerned about what is happening and feeling consumed by it. Overwhelming anxiety goes past awareness and into something that disrupts our ability to engage in our daily lives. We wake up dreading the day before it has even begun. When joy feels completely inaccessible, we find ourselves mentally rehearsing a worst-case scenario in a loop that runs on its own, whether you want it to or not.

Military families, people connected to the conflict, or those who carry unresolved trauma from their own history find that wartime news triggers responses that reach well beyond ordinary worry. The result is that our minds draw connections between what is happening in the present and old wounds that were never fully healed. Suddenly, what we see unfolding across the world feels personal.

The Place Where Faith and Mental Health Meet

Some faith communities believe anxiety is a spiritual problem. The mindset in some of these communities is that praying more, studying the Bible more, and trusting God more will remove the fear that wartime news has created. Spiritual disciplines are valuable, and Scripture speaks to anxiety. The writers of the Psalms were not strangers to wartime, grief, or despair. It was all brought before God, honestly and openly, and without the performance of having it all together.

Anxiety is not eliminated by faith, but the foundation of faith does not shift when everything around you does. Faith offers a perspective that goes beyond the present moment into something eternal. It connects us to a body of believers who are meant to carry each other through the hard seasons. Christian counselors work in a way that integrates the realities of spiritual and psychological thought processes and understand that both matter.

With support, you can learn to handle your anxiety. The key is knowing what to do with it.

Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus. – Philippians 4:6–7, ESV

Finding Your Footing: Practical Steps Toward Overwhelming Anxiety Relief

Navigating overwhelming anxiety is not a one-size-fits-all process. Several practices can help us navigate a world where news is accessible every hour of the day. The first step is to limit our consumption to a defined window during the day and allow our nervous system to settle.

Making time for physical movement helps the body process stress hormones instead of accumulating them. Practices that ground us and redirect our attention to what is present and immediate interrupt the mental loops that keep anxiety running.

During a season of sustained stress and isolation, connection matters. Having honest conversations with a trusted friend or a small group that is not afraid of hard questions can build a defense against the feeling of impending doom.

Christian counselors understand the intersection of faith and mental health. They can encourage you to name what you’ve been quietly carrying. This is the first real step toward something better. Reaching out for help can be difficult, but it is a courageous step toward releasing wartime anxiety.

Hope When You Battle Anxiety

The world has had its share of war, and each generation has faced the challenge of living faithfully amid it. This doesn’t make it easier, and it doesn’t reduce the anxiety or lessen the weight of concern. But it does mean that each of us is not the first person to bring fear and faith into the same room and ask God how to handle them both.

We’re not spiritually deficient or failing. We are human, and we are living through a season that is asking a great deal of each of us.

The great thing is, we don’t have to figure it out alone. There is grace in asking for help from God, who holds all things, and from Christian counselors who are trained, compassionate, and ready to walk alongside us. The possibility of healing from wartime stress and anxiety is in process, and it is in reach no matter when we decide to begin.

If you are experiencing overwhelming anxiety related to wartime stress, or you have a loved one who is grappling with it, there are people to help. Daily life doesn’t have to feel difficult, regardless of what’s happening in the world. You can contact our reception team to schedule a time to meet with a counselor who can help you navigate this season of anxiety.

The Lord your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness; he will quiet you by his love; he will exult over you with loud singing. – Zephaniah 3:17, ESV

item.title: Understanding the Types of BPD and Their Connection to Substance Abuse
item.description:
Borderline personality disorder (BPD) affects how individuals experience themselves and relate to the world around them. Seeking relief from the emotional intensity that comes with BPD, individuals sometimes turn to substance abuse as a common coping mechanism. To understand why some people find themselves caught in patterns that they want to escape, we first have to understand the types of BPD and how they intersect with addiction.

There is a relationship between these two struggles that goes beyond a simple cause-and-effect. It reflects deeper questions about identity, managing pain, and a human need for stability. The way BPD manifests can determine not only how someone experiences their internal world, but which substances they turn to, and why. These distinctions are essential to break free from the cycle of emotional dysregulation and addiction.

Four Patterns Common Across the Multiple Types of BPD

Because each person is unique, borderline personality disorder doesn’t present the same way in everyone. Four primary patterns help explain the different ways that BPD manifests. These types of BPD are not meant to box people into categories concretely, but rather, they help us understand the ways emotional dysregulation shows up in real life. By recognizing which patterns resonate most with an individual, Christian counselors can guide treatment and offer hope that recovery is possible.

The discouraged type: This form of BPD often appears in people who seem dependent and seek constant reassurance while struggling with feelings of worthlessness. These individuals may appear passive or submissive in relationships and avoid confrontation, even when it would be healthy.

The impulsive type: Those who manifest this type of BPD often engage in risk-taking behaviors and emotional outbursts without concern for consequences. People who struggle with this form of BPD typically act on every feeling without pausing to consider the outcome, and they chase experiences that provide immediate gratification or distraction from inner emptiness.

The petulant type: This form of BPD involves stubborn negativity and feeling misunderstood, which results in pushing others away by simultaneously fearing abandonment. Individuals struggling with this pattern often feel like victims of their circumstances and may express bitterness or resentment toward those trying to help.

The self-destructive type: This pattern of BPD manifests in harmful behaviors directed inward, which include substance abuse, self-harm, or extreme risk-taking to manage unbearable emotional pain. Individuals of this type are the most visibly concerning. They seem intent on destroying themselves, even though self-harm isn’t about wanting to die. It’s about making internal pain visible.

Each of these patterns reflects a different strategy for managing the emotional dysregulation that is at the heart of BPD. Many individuals display characteristics from multiple types, and patterns can shift over time, so these categories are not considered rigid.

The consistency across these patterns is the intense fear of abandonment, unstable self-image, and difficulty regulating emotions that define the disorder. Adding substance abuse to this already intense struggle starts as an attempt to navigate the emotional turbulence that feels impossible to manage any other way.

Why Substance Abuse Co-Occurs with BPD

The connection between BPD and addiction is not coincidental. Most individuals diagnosed with BPD also struggle with substance use disorders. Because BPD creates an emotionally intense environment, substances often offer temporary relief from these struggles.

An individual experiencing rapid mood swings, chronic feelings of emptiness, and a fear of abandonment turns to alcohol or other substances to quiet the internal chaos. Substances only provide a brief escape from emotions that feel overwhelming and unmanageable.

Self-medication is not the only challenge with substance abuse and BPD. The brain chemistry is changed due to substance use, which can worsen BPD symptoms and create a cycle where each issue amplifies the other. Impulsivity is a core feature of BPD, and it can become more pronounced under the influence of substances, and emotional regulation becomes nearly impossible.

Christian counselors recognize that both conditions require integrated treatment. They emphasize that addressing one only leaves the underlying vulnerabilities untouched. The path to healing requires understanding how these struggles reinforce each other and learning how to cultivate healthier ways to cope with emotional pain. One good place to start is with encouraging Scriptures:

Cast your burden upon the Lord and He will sustain you; He will never allow the righteous to be shaken. – Psalm 55:22, NASB

How Different Types of BPD Influence Substance Use Patterns

A specific pattern of BPD often shapes the relationship an individual has with substances. Impulsive-type individuals engage in binge drinking or experiment with multiple substances, trying to find a thrill and temporary relief from boredom or inner emptiness.

Individuals who struggle with the self-destructive type of BPD may use substances deliberately to harm themselves or engage in dangerous combinations of risky behaviors. They are less concerned with pleasure and more focused on punishing themselves or numbing severe emotional pain.

Individuals who struggle with the discouraged type often use substances to cope with feelings of hopelessness and inadequacy. Using substances becomes an internal coping mechanism to numb the discouraging feelings.

The individual who suffers from the petulant type of BPD faces a more complex dynamic when it comes to substance use. They may engage in substance use in response to a perceived rejection or conflict. The result is a pattern where relationship struggles trigger substance use, which creates more relationship problems.

Christian counselors understand these patterns and can develop treatment approaches that address the specific needs of each individual who struggles with substance use and BPD. The goal is to build healthier ways to manage emotional experiences that made substances feel necessary in the first place.

Still, we are all reminded of Jesus’ words:

“Come to Me, all who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest.” – Matthew 11:28, NASB

The Path Toward Integrated Healing

Co-occurring BPD and substance abuse recovery requires addressing both conditions simultaneously. If BPD remains untreated, traditional addiction treatment fails because the emotional dysregulation continues to drive the compulsion toward substances.

On the other hand, if BPD is treated without addressing active addiction, the treatment is ineffective because substances interfere with the ability to develop healthy coping strategies. Through integrated treatment, individuals learn to recognize that these conditions exist in relationship to one another and must be addressed together.

Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) has become an effective treatment plan for individuals dealing with both BPD and substance abuse. Through this approach, individuals learn specific skills to manage distress, tolerate stress, and build more effective relationships.

Christian counselors often integrate faith-based perspectives and evidence-based treatments to help clients understand their value in Christ as they develop practical tools to manage symptoms. This process involves learning that emotions do not have to be escaped or numbed. Even intense emotions can be experienced, understood, and regulated in healthy ways.

Finding the Support You Need

The relationship between BPD and substance abuse is a reflection of a human tendency to seek relief from pain through whatever feels available. For treatment to be effective, individuals must understand the different patterns of BPD and how they intersect with addiction.

Each type of BPD – the discouraged, the impulsive, the petulant, or the self-destructive – presents a unique challenge and strength in the recovery process. The consistency is the need for integrated treatment that addresses both the emotional dysregulation involved with BPD and addictive patterns.

Healthy recovery includes building new skills, developing healthier coping mechanisms, and discovering that lasting peace isn’t found by escaping emotions. Instead, you can learn to navigate feelings with grace, support, and God’s Word.

If you or someone you know is facing the complex challenges of BPD and substance abuse, professional support can make a meaningful difference in your recovery. Christian counselors are trained to integrate faith-based encouragement with evidence-based treatment to help you navigate this journey and find lasting recovery.
